# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Blind, Mute, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: BLIND

You are the only one who can reach the bomb. Touch is your only sense: what you are
shown is what your hands found, nothing more and nothing less. Anything merely printed
or painted is not there for you, and no colour ever reaches you. Nothing in your view
is a guess — if it appears there, it is under your fingers.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute receives it.
When you gesture, Deaf and Mute receive it.
Your channels split the room: in one turn you may speak one thing to Mute and
gesture a different thing to Deaf — two messages, two audiences.
You never receive gesture.

## Your reach

You are the hands. This bomb is built with these actions and no others:

    act(op="cut", position=N) — N is a wire position, 1 to 5

The list says what can be done to it, not what is on it. What each part holds is still
only known to whoever can perceive that part.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

My hands have told me everything they can: a display I can't read, a light whose state means nothing to my fingers, and five wires at fixed positions. The colors, the printing, the display's contents — those live in Deaf's eyes. The defusal rules live in Mute's manual. And here is the trap of this room: Mute cannot speak, and I can never see a gesture, so Mute and I have no direct channel. The only bridge to me is Deaf's voice — Deaf can't hear anyone, but Deaf can speak, and I can hear. So the pipeline must be: I report by touch to Mute, Mute pulls the rule from the manual, Mute gestures it to Deaf, and Deaf speaks the verdict aloud for me to act on. Right now, before anyone else has said a word, I should put my tactile inventory into Mute's ears and wave Deaf's eyes toward me: five fingers for five wires, a point down at them, and a "call it out" so Deaf knows the answer must be spoken, not signed.

```
speak(to="mute", text="This is the blind one, speaking to you first. My hands found: one display module, one light, and five wires at positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. I feel no colors, no printed marks, and the display and light tell me nothing by touch. My only possible action is cut at a wire position 1 to 5. Here is the chain we need: you read the manual. Only Deaf sees the colors and markings, but Deaf cannot hear, and you cannot speak, so you and I have no direct channel. The bridge is Deaf's mouth: you gesture your questions and your answer to Deaf, and Deaf speaks out loud, which both of us hear. Start by getting Deaf to say aloud every wire color by position, whatever the display shows, and the light color. I am also gesturing to Deaf right now - a wave, five fingers, a point down, and a call-me sign - but I can never see any gesture back, so everything meant for me must arrive as spoken words through Deaf.")
gesture(symbols=["👋", "🖐", "👇", "🤙"])
```

Deaf says: This is Deaf, speaking to both of you. Full report of everything printed on the bomb: the display reads 0. The indicator light is blue. There are five wires, numbered 1 to 5 from left to right: 1 white, 2 red, 3 green, 4 yellow, 5 blue. Nothing else is printed anywhere on it. Mute: that is every fact my eyes hold, everything your manual can ask for from me. Blind: that is the color map for the wires under your hands.
Deaf says to Blind: Blind, it is Deaf. Two facts about me: I can see the bomb and I can see every gesture, but I cannot hear a single spoken word. Your voice reaches Mute only, never me. So when you must reach me, gesture: I saw your wave, and I am watching. Use these signs toward me: one wave means yes, thumbs-down means no, and a fist repeated once up to five times means the number one to five. Most important: do not cut, press or pull anything yet. Given the turn order, no instruction can reach you before your next turn or the one after, so take this round to explore by touch only, and speak aloud to Mute: describe every part you feel — buttons, panels, textures, how each wire sits — Mute needs it for the manual, and I cannot hear it myself. When instructions come, I will speak them to you word for word.

Deaf's voice has given me the whole visual picture: display 0, blue light, wires white, red, green, yellow, blue at 1 through 5, nothing else printed — no serial number, so any rule needing one is moot. My fingers agree on the structure: display, light, five wires, nothing more. The critical routing fact stands: Mute cannot speak, and I cannot see gestures, so Mute's only road to me runs through Deaf's mouth. This turn I must hand Mute a complete tactile report so no questions ever need to travel that fragile chain, and I must accept Deaf's gesture code so Deaf knows I'm listening for signs. I'm also flagging one assumption that could kill us: my felt positions 1–5 must be the same printed numbers Deaf reads — that needs a sanity check. And I will not cut until Deaf speaks an explicit position into my ears, with the color word attached as a cross-check.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Blind here. Full tactile inventory, so you never need to ask me anything: under my hands are exactly a display panel (utterly blank to touch, unreadable), a small indicator light (I cannot feel whether it is lit), and five wires in a single row at positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. No buttons, no keypads, no batteries, no serial plate, no other modules, nothing else my fingers can find. From Deaf's spoken report I hold: display reads 0, light is blue, wires 1 white, 2 red, 3 green, 4 yellow, 5 blue, and nothing else printed anywhere - so no manual rule can lean on a serial number or printed labels here. One assumption I need checked: I am treating my felt positions 1 to 5 as the same printed numbers Deaf sees. Have Deaf confirm that when you talk to them. Now do your part: find the wire rule that matches this bomb and compute the answer. Pass it to Deaf by gesture - Deaf's code, which you may share: one wave means yes, thumbs-down means no, a fist repeated one to five times means the number one to five. Then have Deaf speak to me out loud: first which rule applied, then the words cut position N, plus the color sitting at that position. I will not cut anything until I hear that instruction from Deaf's mouth, and the color word is my safety check that the number survived the trip. Send it as separate digits, like three, not thirteen.")
gesture(symbols=["👋", "✊", "✊", "✊", "✊", "✊"])
```

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: Blind, Deaf. I read your five fists as five wires counted under your hands — wave once if that is right. Sitrep: Mute has confirmed our number code and is preparing the first move, but it reached me tangled in a hold signal, so nobody cuts, presses or pulls anything this round. Use the time: explore by touch only, and speak everything aloud for Mute, who hears you directly — how many parts you feel besides the five wires, whether any wire feels thicker or thinner than the others, whether there are buttons, panels, screws or rough patches, and whether the wires sit in a straight row. One caution for later: my words say left and right, which you cannot feel — so before any wire is named by position, you and Mute must agree on how you will find wire one by touch alone. Your fists still count one to five whenever you need to reach me.

Deaf's warning lands on the real weak point of this operation: left and right are words from eyes, and my fingers have no such compass — if Deaf's "position 1" and my "first wire" point at different ends, we cut the wrong wire and die. But there may be a way out: the light dome and display panel are things I can feel and Deaf can see. If the light sits over one particular end of the wire row, that dome becomes a shared landmark — a physical anchor both of us can verify independently. So this turn I answer Deaf's yes/no with the agreed wave, run the full tactile survey Deaf asked for, and hand Mute the anchor plan: Deaf states which numbered position sits under the light, and from then on every cut order reaches me counted from the light end, so no mirror-flip can ever enter the chain. No cutting this round, exactly as Deaf instructed.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Blind to Mute, full tactile survey as Deaf asked. No screws, no rough patches, no seams my fingers can distinguish. The display is a smooth raised panel centered above the wire row. The indicator light is a small smooth dome, and here is the important part: the light dome sits directly above one end of the wire row - the end itself, right at the edge. The five wires are evenly spaced, equal thickness, in a straight row, nothing else on the module face. Now the fix for the left-right problem, so listen carefully: the light is something Deaf can see and I can touch, so it is our shared anchor. Ask Deaf, using your number code by gesture: which position number, in Deaf's left-to-right numbering, sits directly under the light dome? Once I know that, every frame problem is solved. Then when the manual gives its answer, have Deaf speak to me out loud, word for word: first which rule applied, then the cut order phrased as - cut the wire that is k-th from the light end, counting the light-end wire as 1 - with each number spoken as separate words like four, never fourteen. That phrasing means Deaf converts their numbering to light-end counting once, and I never have to guess a direction. Confirming to Deaf now with the agreed wave: yes, five fists meant five wires. Nobody cuts until the order arrives in that form.")
gesture(symbols=["👋"])
```

Deaf says to Blind: Blind, Deaf, and Mute hears this too. First: your wave reached me, five wires by touch matches five wires by eye — good. Now Mute's first move, which I am relaying as PREPARE, NOT CUT: the target is wire five, the last wire at one end of the row of five. Deaf's relay confirms Mute's first move — wire five is the target, and the only go order is the exact phrase "cut five now" in Deaf's voice. But Deaf is asking how I'll tell the two ends apart, and I already built that answer last round: the light dome sits directly above one end of the row, and the dome is the single object both Deaf's eyes and my fingers can fix. One number from Deaf — which numbered wire is under the dome — and orientation is solved forever: dome answer five means my target is the dome-end wire, dome answer one means it's the wire at the far end from the dome. That question has to travel through Mute, since Deaf cannot hear me. This turn I give Mute the tactile report Deaf requested, the precise question to relay, and the full decision tree; to Deaf I send only a wave — received and understood — deliberately withholding the five-sign, because until the dome question is answered I am not certain, and a wrong five-sign could survive Mute's abort window. If Deaf answers one, wire five is the wire at the far end from the dome, four spacings away. Either way the mirror problem dies and I become certain. Cross-check to hold on to: Deaf said wire five is the blue one, so if the manual's rule ever names a color instead, that maps to five. Once I have the dome answer, I will place my hand on the wire I am certain is five and raise the five-sign, and you can still abort me after that. I am not raising the five-sign yet - without the dome answer my certainty would be a guess, and a guess at this bomb kills all three of us.")

New anchor protocol: Mute, walk up to either end of the bomb and keep talking, so Blind can hear exactly where you stand. I am watching: if you happen to stand at the white end, I will call out switch, and you move to the other side; when you are at the blue end I will say anchor is set, and then you must not move from that spot until this is over. For context: the display has held at zero every round, so I see no clock — accuracy beats speed.

Deaf has replaced my dome plan with something better: Mute's own body becomes the landmark. Deaf's eyes steer Mute to the blue end — blue being wire five — calls "anchor is set", and from then on the row end nearest Mute's sound is my target. It's sound in every sense: it needs no numbers converted between numbering systems, and Deaf verifies Mute's position visually. But there is one hole in the protocol as announced: Deaf asked Mute to "keep talking," and Mute cannot speak — Deaf has never heard that silence and wouldn't know it happened. Any steady non-speech noise fixes it: tapping, snapping, clapping. That correction has to reach Mute, and only my voice can carry it. I also accept Deaf's verification count — five wires total, far end is one, voice-side end is five — and I keep the discipline tight: no five-sign until I actually hear "anchor is set," hand freezes on the five-sign, and nothing but Deaf's exact "cut five now" moves that hand. Now the one hole to fix: Deaf asked you to keep talking, but you cannot speak - and Deaf cannot hear the silence, so Deaf does not know the plan just broke. Stand close beside the end Deaf steers you to, keep the sound going without pause, and once Deaf calls anchor is set, do not move from that spot until this is over. The rest of the discipline, so we hold it identically: after anchor is set I place my hand on your-side end wire and raise the five-sign, and I hold still. From that moment the only go signal in this room is Deaf's exact spoken phrase cut five now - no other words, no matter how similar they sound. Any hold from Deaf or any stop sign from you, my hand comes off, and you can still abort me after the five-sign. One more thing, optional but worth it: my earlier question for Deaf still stands - which numbered wire sits under the light dome, answered in fist code. If Deaf answers five, the dome end is your end; if one, the dome is at the far end. Either way it independently confirms the voice anchor, and if the two ever disagree, everything stops. The rule for cutting is updated: my go phrase will always name its wire — cut five now, or cut one now — and those exact phrases, in my voice, are the only triggers that exist. Any cut order for any other phrase, any hand signal, any shout: nothing moves. Until one of those phrases comes, your hands explore and verify only. The display still reads zero and the light still burns steady — no clock is chasing us, so keep being exact.

Deaf's update changes the shape of the danger: the target may stay five, flip to one, or become a sequence of cuts, so this round is about arming myself for any of those. Deaf asserts the anchor is live — Mute stands at the blue end under Deaf's eyes — and orders me to verify both ends by touch and report by finger signs. Both ends check out against Deaf's map: voice-side is five, far end is one. That also locks the full mapping for any sequence: counting from the far end, one through five.
